articles.author: Alexandru Cazan
articles.description:
Originally published at tothenoc.substack.com
A check that cannot fail is not a check.
Last week a check told me there was nothing new in my mailbox. There were four messages that mattered, all from that same day. The check did not fail. It ran, it filtered, it returned an empty list. The filter compared dates written as text, and the text did not match. Empty, no error. I caught it by reading the mailbox myself.
It was not the first time. Same family, different tools, all on our own systems:
a search over the mail server returned zero results. The mailboxes are stored compressed. The search read the raw files, found nothing, and said so politely.
an upgrade script exited with code 0, one second after it started. It had checked who was running it, did not like the answer, and quietly did nothing.
a daily report came out as a file of zero bytes. Its output path pointed to a folder that had been archived the night before.
None of these crashed. A crash is easy, somebody sees it. The dangerous result is the one that looks exactly like good news: nothing found, nothing changed, nothing to report.
What we do now:
every check has a positive control, a known item it must find. If the check cannot find the thing I know is there, its zero means nothing,
a result that came back too fast is not a result. Zero hits on a full disk in zero seconds is a tool that did not look,
read the log, not the exit code. Code 0 says the program ended. It does not say what it did,
a report has a last line that says it finished. No last line, no report.
"Nothing new" is a claim. Before you believe it, ask how the check would look if something was new.
If you are deciding who watches this for you, this is what to ask: what an outsourced NOC actually covers, and what it costs.
-- Alex
articles.title: Nothing new. Exit code 0.

Moving DNS and email into one control plane can reduce integration work, but it cannot establish that a customer's inbound mail reaches the intended mailbox. The page fires because invoice search has stopped finding recent orders. On-call sees successful uploads, no missing originals, and a growing interval between uploaded_at and text_stored_at. The customer-facing symptom arrived late: the useful alert was the age of the oldest accepted invoice still waiting for OCR.
Short answer: accept and validate the uploaded scan, store the original under its document ID, enqueue OCR, then persist extracted text and confidence separately. Keep the original so a template change or a better extractor can trigger reprocessing. Alert on queue age against the search-availability SLO, not merely on OCR errors. Running OCR inline on a large scan makes the upload request inherit OCR latency and timeout risk.

articles.description:
If you run Java workloads on Kubernetes, you have probably stared at slow pod readiness metrics during a deployment or autoscaling event. While the JVM is unmatched for long-running throughput, its cold-start tax—spent loading, verifying, and linking thousands of classes—can make scaling painful.
The usual advice is to compile your application into a GraalVM Native Image. That delivers sub-second startups, but it comes at a steep operational price: long build times, closed-world reflection constraints, and breaking changes to existing Java agents and libraries.
OpenJDK offers a middle ground: Application Class-Data Sharing (AppCDS) on JDK 21+ and Project Leyden AOT caches on JDK 25+. These features let the JVM dump its internal class metadata into a pre-linked archive file on disk, allowin…
articles.title: Faster Java Pod Startups Without GraalVM: Why AppCDS Needs Kubernetes Image Volumes

Not because it's bad. Because there's too much of it. That's the quiet problem with agentic coding nobody talks about.
The agents got faster. Our attention didn't.
The bottleneck isn't the model anymore. It's me, scroll…

articles.author: AI Client Discovery
articles.description:
Reproduced in my own test setup — not a client's, and no real account involved:
The setup: a test endpoint receives the webhook, parses the JSON body, then
What actually breaks it: the signature is computed over the exact bytes that
The fix, in order:
Capture the raw request body as bytes BEFORE any JSON parsing, and verify
the signature against those bytes only. In most frameworks that means
reading the raw body / disabling the JSON body parser on the webhook route. Only after verification passes, parse the body and process the event. If your platform parses the body for you before your code runs (some
no-code webhook steps do), check whether it offers a "raw body" output —
if it doesn't, verify at a step that still sees the raw payload, or move
verification to a small endpoint that does.
How to tell this apart from a genuinely wrong secret: compute the HMAC
One gotcha while testing: don't "verify" by re-sending from a tool that
re-serializes the payload for you — you'll reproduce the failure and conclude
the secret is wrong. Test against the exact bytes the sender sent.
articles.title: Webhook signature verification fails even though the secret is right

articles.description:
My father-in-law lives alone. What my wife actually wants to know, ten times a day, is one boring thing: is he up and moving around the flat? Not his pulse. Not a video feed. Just: did the shape of the room change in the last few minutes.
Every product we looked at solved it with a camera or a wearable. Both fail for the same reason: he will not wear a watch to bed, and he unplugged the camera on day three because he does not want to be watched in his own home.
So we built the thing around the constraint instead of around the sensor. No lens, no microphone, no device on the body.
Wi-Fi is not just a carrier, it is a probe. A body in a room changes the multipath between two fixed nodes: some subcarriers get absorbed, some arrive out of phase. Sample the channel state at a fixed rate and the…
